summary: A response to claims in several mail and FTP RFCs that network mail should be free, meaning that no login should be required. Padlipsky argues that free does not have to mean login-less: explicit login to a free account could be more natural on some systems. It is a discussion of a design choice.

eli5.summary: People said mail should be free to send, and this author says that does not mean no sign-in. A guest account would work too.

questions: what is free in network mail
subtitle: Padlipsky argues that free network mail does not have to mean no login, and proposes USER NETML.

tldr.problem: Several mail and FTP RFCs (454, 475, 479) asserted that network mail should be free, meaning no login or USER command should be required.
tldr.mechanism: Padlipsky argues an explicit login to a free account also works and may suit some hosts better, and proposes that USER NETML and PASS NETML work everywhere for free mail, with a new FTP FREE command as a fallback.
tldr.outcome: It is a position paper on a design choice, not a specification.

today: The status in the unit data is Unknown and no replacing RFC is recorded. It is a 1973 position paper on one design question raised by RFC 475.

sections.title: What Free Means
sections.content:
Three RFCs about mail and FTP (454, 475 and 479) say something like "Network mail should be free; i.e., no login or USER command should be required." The author says the "i.e." is misleading: mail could also be free through an explicit login on a free account, which may be more natural depending on how a host's logger or process creation works.

The drawback is that users must remember the free account's name, which is a small burden if the account has the same name everywhere.
sections.eli5: Free does not have to mean no sign-in. It can mean everyone signs in to the same free guest account.

sections.title: The NETML Proposal
sections.content:
The proposal: network mail should be free and should not require users to remember the free account's name. It should either be "loginless" or use the same login everywhere. Because some systems prefer a login, USER NETML and PASS NETML should work everywhere for free mail.

The name NETML is fewer than six characters and upper case, so it fits the least common denominator of user identifiers, and it is unlikely to clash with anyone's initials.

If NETML were repugnant to some hosts, a new FTP FREE command is proposed so servers need not treat MAIL as an implicit login.
sections.eli5: Everyone would sign in as the same guest, NETML, so nobody has to remember a special name.

sections.title: Authentication and Accounting
sections.content:
The "loginless" view assumes the sole purpose of login is to start accounting. On a system with access control on mailboxes, the process's principal identifier, set at login, must match an entry on the mailbox's access control list. The author says accounting should perhaps be separated from authentication, but not always, so inventing a redundant mechanism like a FROM command (suggested in RFC 475) is questionable.

He adds that if MAIL implied a login, the growing list of such commands would force server changes, and it would be hard to pass arguments to the process created for the mailer. He also notes that FTP is internally inconsistent: the USER command acknowledges that some systems require USER and PASS, while the mail discussion says they may not.
sections.eli5: Signing in is how a computer knows who you are. Making a second way to say who you are just adds extra work.
